title: Family_Lagrangian_Workbench.ipynb

canonical_node.axiom: The Lowe Coherence Lagrangian (LLC) is a legitimate dynamical system that remains stable across randomized parameter configurations.
definitions: Lowe Coherence Lagrangian (LLC): L(q, q) =  chi(q) * q K q  V(q), where chi(q) is the coherence function (product of all 10 variable contributions), K is the 1010 kinetic matrix with symmetry pair couplings, and V(q) = S * chi(q) is the entropic potential.
Pass rate: fraction of tests passed in a given model evaluation.
Stress sweep: 60 independent builds with randomized weights, pair strength, confinement, and chi parameters.
derivation: The LLC is defined with a coherence function chi(q) multiplying the kinetic term and an entropic potential V(q) = S*chi(q).
Euler-Lagrange equations are derived from L, yielding equations of motion where every variable influences every other through chi.
The notebook runs the LLC against standard models (harmonic oscillator, coupled oscillator pair) and then performs a 60-run stress sweep with randomized parameters.
Results: mean pass rate 0.858 across the stress sweep; mass matrix full-rank and positive definite in all tested configurations; energy drift 8.22e-9 for LLC.
One test failure (zeroing variables suppresses chi) is explicitly noted and explained as a sensitivity spike, not a proof of product-irreducibility.
canonical_node.action: The system should treat the LLC as a stable dynamical system candidate, subject to further validation, and use the stress sweep methodology as a template for testing other proposed Lagrangians.
boundary: This document does not prove the LLC produces physically meaningful predictions beyond stability; it only demonstrates numerical stability across parameter variations.
The 85.8% pass rate is not a proof of physical correctness; it is a stress test result.
The document does not claim the LLC is the correct theory of everything; it only claims it is not fragile.
test: Run the 60-run stress sweep with randomized parameters and verify mean pass rate  0.85.
Check that the mass matrix is full-rank and positive definite across all tested configurations.
Verify energy drift is below a numerically negligible threshold (e.g., < 1e-8).
Confirm that the one known failure (zeroing variables suppresses chi) is reproducible and correctly interpreted.

dg1_dependencies: Standard physics models (harmonic oscillator, coupled oscillator pair) as benchmarks.
Numerical methods for solving Euler-Lagrange equations and computing energy drift.
Random parameter generation for stress sweep.
dg_protocol.dg2_new_capability: Provides a stress-testing protocol for evaluating the stability of a proposed Lagrangian across randomized parameter configurations, yielding a quantitative pass rate and matrix properties.
dg_protocol.dg3_preserved_floor: Preserves the mathematical structure of the LLC and the standard benchmark models; does not alter the underlying equations.
dg_protocol.dg4_collapse_if_removed: If this document is removed, the LLC loses its empirical stability evidence, reducing it to an untested theoretical construct.

classification.recommended_atom_action: preserve as evidence of stability; do not upgrade to proof of physical validity

overstatement_risks: Interpreting the 85.8% pass rate as proof of physical correctness rather than numerical stability.
Treating the LLC as validated physics without independent theoretical derivation.
Ignoring the one test failure and its explanation.
kill_conditions: If the stress sweep is not reproducible with the same pass rate.
If the mass matrix is found not positive definite in some configuration.
If the energy drift is not numerically negligible.
risk.lean_target: Formalize the stress sweep as a reusable Lean theorem about the stability of a class of Lagrangians with coherence functions.

plain_summary: This document reports a stress test of the Lowe Coherence Lagrangian (LLC) using a 60-run randomized parameter sweep. It shows the LLC is stable across many configurations, with a mean pass rate of 85.8%, a full-rank positive definite mass matrix, and low energy drift. However, this is empirical evidence of stability, not a proof of physical correctness. The document is honest about one test failure and does not overclaim.
